clue.text: Ahead of the game appeal stalls against City

indicators.note: one thing placed ahead of another simply comes before it in the line
to stall an animal is to shut it inside a stall, so one piece is housed within another

blocks.note: SA is the crossword abbreviation for sex appeal
Go is the Japanese board game
anti means against

explanation.surface: A crowd-pleasing appeal holds things up just before a match against a city side.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stalls' looks like a noun for theatre seats but is a verb: the first two pieces, joined, hold the third after their opening letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Santiago is the capital of Chile, so it is an example of the broad category named.

clue.text: What’s articulated intermittently by “amen” in half-hearted note?

definitions.text: What’s articulated intermittently by “amen” in half-hearted note?
definitions.note: the whole clue describes something sung and closed by an amen

indicators.note: speaking only now and then keeps every other letter and drops the rest
a word with a doubled centre loses half of that heart, one of its two middle letters
the chosen letters go inside the other piece

blocks.note: to note is to heed, pay attention; half its heart goes, one of the two middle letters
the even letters of BY AMEN

explanation.surface: A question about what a congregation chants, bit by bit, around its closing amen.
explanation.walkthrough: HEED loses one E to leave HED, and the even letters Y, M, N from 'by amen' sit inside it. Read whole, the clue also describes a hymn sung with an amen at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Something hymned has been sung in praise, as church verses finishing with a closing amen are.

clue.text: Foot of The Sun’s front page carries first of items on counter-intelligence

indicators.note: the foot of a word is where it ends, so only its final letter is kept
the front of a word is its opening letter alone
the first of a word is just its opening letter
whatever carries a load holds it within itself

blocks.note: the last letter of THE
the opening letter of SUN
used as printed, holding the next two pieces
the opening letter of ITEMS
used as printed

explanation.surface: A tabloid front page runs a story at the bottom about secret-service spying.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On' and 'page' are used exactly as printed, which is easy to miss. The Sun is a British tabloid newspaper.
explanation.definitionFit: Spying on rival states is the world that counter-intelligence works in, so the setter treats them as loosely equivalent.

clue.text: Man-about-town is a cock, according to Mr Ross

indicators.note: the broadcaster Jonathan Ross famously cannot sound his Rs, so we hear a word as he would say it

blocks.note: a cock is a rooster, and Ross turns its opening R into a W

explanation.surface: A TV host jokes that a young man-about-town is a cocky show-off.
explanation.walkthrough: Jonathan Ross is a British TV presenter nicknamed Wossy for his rhotacism. Bertie Wooster is P G Wodehouse's idle gentleman.
explanation.definitionFit: Bertie Wooster, of Wodehouse's Jeeves stories, is the classic idle young gentleman living it up in London society.

clue.text: My Latin picked up here?

definitions.note: the whole clue points to the country where Latin began

indicators.note: letters picked out of a phrase are taken from within it
in a down entry, going up means reading the letters from the bottom

blocks.note: read backwards, MYLATIN holds the letters needed

explanation.surface: Someone muses that they learnt their Latin here, perhaps on holiday.
explanation.walkthrough: Reading MY LATIN backwards gives NITALYM, with the country inside it. Read whole, Latin is the language of ancient Rome.
explanation.definitionFit: Latin was the tongue of ancient Rome, so its homeland is the obvious place a person would acquire it.

clue.text: Out of shackles, so old Terry Venables stays away from the ground

indicators.note: stays are a corset, which grips whatever sits inside it
moving away from the ground in a down entry means rising, so the letters read upwards

blocks.note: El Tel was the tabloid nickname of the football manager
used as printed
O is the standard abbreviation for old

explanation.surface: A former England football manager, freed of shackles, keeps away from the stadium.
explanation.walkthrough: Terry Venables managed England, and the tabloids called him El Tel. The whole assembled string then reads upwards, since a down entry climbing leaves the ground.
explanation.definitionFit: Something freed from chains or restraint has been released, which is exactly the idiomatic sense of the phrase.

clue.text: Ultimately derived from ill-will, to actively hate?

definitions.text: Ultimately derived from ill-will, to actively hate?
definitions.note: the whole clue describes the feeling

indicators.note: what comes ultimately from a word is its very end, the final letter
active things keep moving about, so these letters get rearranged

blocks.note: the final letter of ILL-WILL
the final letter of TO
anagram fodder, four letters

explanation.surface: A question: does real hatred grow out of lingering ill-will?
explanation.walkthrough: L and O are the last letters of 'ill-will' and 'to'; HATE rearranged follows. Read whole, the clue describes that deep hostility.
explanation.definitionFit: To feel intense, active dislike born of bitterness is to detest, the strongest everyday verb for enmity.

clue.text: Spirited away to the East Side after school

indicators.note: in an across entry east is the right-hand end, so only a word's final letter is kept
one piece comes after another in the line

blocks.note: a gam is a school of whales
the final letter of AWAY

explanation.surface: A child is spirited off to New York's East Side straight after school.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spirited away' reads as one phrase but splits: 'Spirited' is the definition and 'away' gives its last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Gamy (or gamey) can mean plucky and full of fight, like a game bird, so it matches lively courage.

clue.text: Stereotyped pet seen swallowing (just) head of pig

indicators.note: what is swallowed ends up inside the swallower
only the leading letter goes inside, so the remainder is left trailing afterwards

blocks.note: seen means spotted
a hog is a pig; only its first letter is swallowed

explanation.surface: A cartoonish stock pet is spotted gulping down a pig's head.
explanation.walkthrough: The brackets matter: only the pig's first letter goes inside, and the rest of the animal trails after. Spot is the dog in Eric Hill's picture books.
explanation.definitionFit: Spot is the stock name for a dog, so a pet called that is a cliché, a typecast animal.

clue.text: They may be kept in the kitchen cabinet, unless it shatters
One that was appreciated getting behind very funny novel

indicators.note: whatever gets behind something follows it in the line

blocks.note: LOL, laugh out loud, is text-speak for very funny
I is the Roman numeral one
ta is British slang for thanks

explanation.surface: A reader thanks someone for backing a hilarious book.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One that was appreciated' reads as a single thing but is two: I, then TA, which Britons say for thanks.
explanation.definitionFit: Lolita is Vladimir Nabokov's 1955 book, a famous and controversial work of fiction.

clue.text: One whose act will entertain and carpet will spoil!

indicators.note: spoiling something ruins its arrangement, leaving the letters jumbled

blocks.note: anagram fodder, nine letters

explanation.surface: A performer's routine delights the audience but ruins the rug underfoot.
explanation.walkthrough: Read whole, the joke works too: metal-tipped shoes clattering on a carpet would damage it.
explanation.definitionFit: A performer in metal-plated shoes whose rhythmic footwork is a stage turn meant to delight audiences.

clue.text: Somewhere shady I’ll be on the fiddle

definitions.note: a whimsical description of a person, one who bows

blocks.note: a leafy arbour giving shade
a violinist draws a bow across the strings

explanation.surface: A crook boasts of a dodgy hideaway where they will run their fiddles.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On the fiddle' is British slang for cheating, but here it is the violin: one who bows it.
explanation.definitionFit: A shaded garden retreat under leafy branches, and whimsically a person who draws a bow across strings.

clue.text: Vera? The rest is 28

blocks.note: the surface reading: a woman's name, perhaps someone telling a story
the setter's reading: VERA is the first half of an eight-letter word for honesty, and the remainder is the answer at 28 across

explanation.walkthrough: VERACITY means truthfulness; VERA is its first four of eight letters. The rest refers to 28 across, LIES, the other half of such a statement.
explanation.definitionFit: A statement with only partial honesty, leaving out enough to mislead, is what this compound noun names.

clue.text: Getting very wet, they think about adopting alias

indicators.note: turning about is facing the other way, so the letters run backwards
adopting someone takes them into the household, so one piece goes inside another

blocks.note: egos are the thinking selves
aka, also known as, introduces an alias

explanation.surface: People caught in a downpour mull over taking on false names.
explanation.walkthrough: 'They think' is a cryptic noun phrase for the conscious selves that do the thinking, turned round before it takes in the alias.
explanation.definitionFit: Soakage is the process of absorbing liquid, a noun for becoming saturated, so it matches a thorough drenching.

clue.text: Lady Gaga Inn, set in one thousand acres?

indicators.note: someone gaga is muddled, so these letters are scrambled
a stone set in a ring sits within it

blocks.note: K is the abbreviation for a thousand
acres are an example of area, hence the question mark
anagram fodder, three letters

explanation.surface: A pub named for Lady Gaga stands in its own thousand acres of grounds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lady Gaga' splits: 'Lady' is the definition and 'Gaga' the anagram signal. Acres are a measure of area, so they stand for it by example.
explanation.definitionFit: Anna Karenina, heroine of Tolstoy's novel, is an aristocrat, so she is an example of a titled woman.

clue.text: China, Japan and more regions covered in feet

indicators.note: whatever is covered sits within its covering

blocks.note: ft is the abbreviation for feet
regions are areas

explanation.surface: Map talk: China, Japan and other lands measured out in feet.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a list of examples, so 'and more' belongs to it rather than to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: The Far East is the traditional Western name for East Asia, the part of the world containing those nations.

clue.text: Athenian Club’s reduced joining fees

indicators.note: a reduced word is cut down to a shortened form
two pieces joining are placed side by side

blocks.note: a club is a society, shortened to its usual abbreviation
fees are rates, charges

explanation.surface: An Athens club has cut its membership subscription.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Athenian Club' looks like the name of a society, but 'Athenian' stands alone as the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Socrates, the classical philosopher, lived his whole life in ancient Athens, so he is an example of its citizens.

clue.text: Fine to waive it, carrying on without charge

indicators.note: waiving something gives it up, so those two letters are dropped
whatever carries a load holds it within

blocks.note: a fine is a forfeit, a penalty
re means on or concerning

explanation.surface: A penalty could be waived, letting things carry on without any cost.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fine' looks like approval but is a penalty, and 'it' is dropped literally from the end of that word before the second piece goes in.
explanation.definitionFit: Getting something at no cost means not paying, which is what the phrase means, a common idiom.

clue.text: Brother of the French Resistance breaks out of jail

indicators.note: breaking into something means getting inside it

blocks.note: someone out of jail is free
R is the physics symbol for resistance

explanation.surface: A wartime French Resistance fighter's brother escapes from prison.
explanation.walkthrough: 'French Resistance' is a famous pairing, but 'French' goes with the definition and 'Resistance' is R.
explanation.definitionFit: In the language of France a male sibling is called frère, so this is a foreign-language translation.

clue.text: Game good – I see Javan rhino?

blocks.note: RU is rugby union
pi, short for pious, means good
ah is an exclamation of understanding

explanation.surface: A game-watcher on safari exclaims at spotting a rare rhinoceros on Java.
explanation.walkthrough: Rhino is old British slang for money, so a Javan rhino is Indonesian cash, not the endangered animal.
explanation.definitionFit: The rupiah is the currency of Indonesia, which includes Java, and rhino is slang for cash.

clue.text: Receiver’s ID that wasn’t intended to upset

definitions.note: a clause; the phrase is said to excuse a remark

blocks.note: an ID can be a number, abbreviated No.
read as 'of fence': a fence receives stolen goods

explanation.surface: A handler of stolen goods insists the identification was not meant as an insult.
explanation.walkthrough: Respaced, the answer reads as a receiver's identifying number; a fence is someone who receives stolen goods.
explanation.definitionFit: People say it after a remark to show they meant no insult, so it stands for a comment meant harmlessly.

clue.text: They block mobile, self-descriptively

indicators.note: the word that signals the jumbling also supplies the letters, describing itself

blocks.note: anagram fodder, six letters, and also the signal to rearrange

explanation.surface: Some devices block mobile phone signals, as their name describes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mobile' does double duty: it is the anagram signal and the fodder at once, which is what 'self-descriptively' tells you.
explanation.definitionFit: Emboli are clots or bubbles carried in the bloodstream that lodge in and obstruct a vessel.

clue.text: Catherine’s favourite who fought – as Meat Loaf would do most things – without armour

indicators.note: armour is an outer shell, so taking it off strips the outside letters

blocks.clueFragment: as Meat Loaf would do most things
blocks.note: Meat Loaf sang 'I'd Do Anything for Love (But I Won't Do That)', so most things, not quite all

explanation.surface: A court favourite battles bare-chested, the way the rock singer would do almost anything.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase from Meat Loaf's song title loses its first and last letters. Grigory Orlov was a guards officer and lover of Catherine the Great.
explanation.definitionFit: Grigory Orlov, a soldier who helped put Catherine the Great on the Russian throne, was her lover for years.

clue.text: The first person named on an envelope?

definitions.note: a whimsical description: the addressee is the one who opens it

blocks.note: the first game or item in a series
the addressee is whoever unseals the letter

explanation.surface: Whose name goes first when addressing an envelope?
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the whimsy: the person named on the envelope is the one who will slit it.
explanation.definitionFit: A season's first match or a show's first act is called that, and so is anyone who unseals post.

clue.text: Addressed to Teddy, could it be someone up the line?

blocks.note: a letter addressed to someone is for them
a teddy is a toy bear, and E. Bear is how Edward Bear, Pooh's formal name, is written on a label

explanation.surface: A parcel labelled for a teddy: might it be for someone further along the queue?
explanation.walkthrough: Read as a label, the answer says 'for Edward Bear', a teddy's formal name, with Edward cut to its initial. 'Up the line' means earlier in a family line.
explanation.definitionFit: An ancestor sits further back in one's family tree, and the word names such a predecessor.

clue.text: What could make best bra home for toucan?

blocks.note: the surface reading: something that makes the finest bra
the setter's reading, split 2,2,3,3: two letters put in place of the final three would turn the word best into bra

explanation.surface: Lingerie talk: what would make the best bra, and where does a toucan live?
explanation.walkthrough: Split as RA IN FOR EST, the answer is an instruction: put RA in place of EST, and BEST becomes BRA.
explanation.definitionFit: Toucans are tropical birds of the dense wet forests of Central and South America, their natural habitat.

clue.text: Matilda’s weakness remains

blocks.note: Hilaire Belloc's cautionary Matilda told such dreadful ones
to remain in place is to stay put

explanation.surface: An old woman named Matilda has one frailty that lingers.
explanation.walkthrough: Belloc's poem 'Matilda, Who Told Lies, and Was Burned to Death' is a British nursery classic. 'Remains' is a verb, not a noun.
explanation.definitionFit: Belloc's Matilda was undone by her untruths, and a thing that stays where it is also rests there.
